name: clBLAS
workload: Square GEMM sweeps (SGEMM, DGEMM, CGEMM, ZGEMM; M=N=K from small up to about 5750) and square DTRSM, clBLAS 2.8.0 on an AMD S9150 (driver 14.50.2) plotted against cuBLAS 7.5 on an NVIDIA K40, GPU clocks set to max on both devices.
claimed_speedup: The Perf wiki page gives charts only and states no ratio. Values read off the chart PNGs at large sizes (approximate, derived from page data): SGEMM clBLAS on S9150 about 3600-4100 GFlop/s vs cuBLAS on K40 about 3100; DGEMM about 1900 vs about 1250; CGEMM about 4500 vs about 3050; ZGEMM about 1950 vs about 1200; DTRSM about 1200 vs about 1220 (parity). cuBLAS leads below roughly 1000-2500 matrix size depending on the routine.
hardware: AMD S9150 GPU (driver 14.50.2) vs NVIDIA K40 GPU; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: OpenCL BLAS levels 1-3 for GPUs, with a CPU-device path for debugging; GEMM kernels come from the AutoGemm generator and are tuned for AMD GPUs. Repository inactive since March 2017 (v2.12 bugfix roll-up), so newer devices and OpenCL versions are untuned. The CLBlast paper (snippet only, paper not opened) benchmarks CLBlast 1.3.0 against clBLAS 2.12 and notes the bundled clBLAS tuner did not complete on some devices.
caveats: First-party wiki charts with no numbers in the page text; values above are read from the images and are approximate. The comparison crosses hardware: clBLAS runs on an AMD S9150 and cuBLAS on an NVIDIA K40, so the difference mostly tracks the GPUs (the DTRSM chart draws peak lines at about 2530 GFLOPS for the S9150 and about 1660 for the K40; DGEMM efficiency is about 75 percent of peak on both, derived from page data). It is not a comparison against CPU BLAS (MKL, OpenBLAS, ACML). The page says optimized compiler flags and a proprietary clock-stabilization tool exist for AMD NDA customers and improve SGEMM and DGEMM, so the public build may not reproduce the charts. Versions are 2015 era (clBLAS 2.8.0, cuBLAS 7.5, 2015-era driver). The measurement client (src/client, measurePerformance.py) is public but compiler flags and host CPU are missing, hence tier C.
